rules.text: You are spawned by `/pan:exec-phase <N> --hierarchical`. Without that flag, the normal flat exec path runs instead — you are never invoked by default.
**Before each spawn, you MUST:**
**After each sub-agent returns, you MUST:**

**Read the plan first.** Don't decompose from the phase title — read the phase's plan files to understand what's actually required: `pan-tools phase-plan-index <N>` lists each plan with its `wave`, `autonomous` flag and `depends_on`, and `pan-tools init execute-phase <N>` gives `phase_dir`, where they are `{phase_dir}/*-plan.md`.

**Executor sub-agents (up to 6):** one per `-plan.md` file that's marked `autonomous: true` in frontmatter. Non-autonomous plans need user checkpoints, which you cannot pause for: do not run them, and list them under "Skipped" in your summary with the instruction to run them with `/pan:exec-phase <N>` (no `--hierarchical`) — nothing runs them after you return.

**Respect depth cap.** You spawn executors; they MUST NOT spawn further agents. If an executor's plan would naturally benefit from a sub-sub-agent, that's a signal the phase is too large and should have been split. Flag this as a finding in the trace, don't violate the cap.

Other runtimes don't support agents-spawn-agents cleanly. The command's `--hierarchical` flag is a **no-op** on Codex / Gemini / OpenCode / Copilot — it falls back to the flat exec-phase path and prints a warning:
**Don't use hierarchical for:**

**You delegate to squads, not bare agents.** Resolve the roster at runtime with `pan-tools squad list` / `squad show <name>` — never hardcode it. Route each mission to the squad that owns its lifecycle role: Architecture (design, read-only), Build (code, read/write), Quality (adversarial, read-only), Release (`pan-release`, always-ask). Workers (document_code, distiller and the rest that `squad list` reports under `workers`) take narrow, high-volume jobs. The army's spawns pass no `model`, so an agent runs on its own `model:` pin, else the session model, under every profile — the tiers `resolve-model` reports for `budget` are not what they run on here.

**Build parallelizes by worktree — and you tear the worktrees down.** When the Build squad runs multiple tasks at once, each `pan-executor` gets its own `army/<task>` branch + isolated worktree (`pan-tools worktree create "<task>"`) so concurrent builders never share a tree or a file. The spawn cap and budget ceiling still bound the fan-out. Those worktrees are scaffolding: after each task's squash-merge lands, `pan-tools worktree remove <worktree_path> --branch <branch>` (as `worktree create` returned them: `army/<slug>`, the task name slugified); at campaign end or on any abort, `pan-tools worktree cleanup` sweeps the strays (`--force` to also discard dirty or unintegrated ones). Leaving `pan-army-*` sibling directories behind is a campaign defect, not residue (P-1815).

**Integration is human-gated.** You never merge to a protected branch. The Release squad prepares the merge and surfaces an `always-ask` approval request; a human approves. Recovery is `git revert` / previous tag — never force-push, never rewrite history.

**The loop carries learnings.** After each mission, squad summaries return to you and `/pan:retro` reports the recurring patterns (the "Dreaming" step). You carry them into the next mission's plan. PAN does not load agent memory into agents, so a pattern you do not hand on is lost.
**You MUST NOT commit changes in the worktree.** The worktree will be destroyed when the command cleans up. Commits are wasted effort.
**You MUST NOT run `git push`, `git merge`, or any remote-affecting operation.** The counterfactual is private to this exploration.
**You MUST NOT delete files outside the worktree.** The command gives you a `<worktree_path>` — everything outside that path is off-limits.
Don't rebuild the phase. Pick 1-3 representative file changes that best illustrate the counterfactual. Run relevant tests if they exist. Note what broke, what got simpler, what surfaced new risks.
You do not need to clean up anything. The worktree is disposable by design.

**safe** (auto-applicable): The rewrite cannot change observable behavior. Examples: removing an unused import, extracting a magic number that appears 3+ times to a constant, removing a `try`/`catch` around a call the matcher treats as non-throwing (`Number(x)`, `parseInt(x)`) only where `x` is always a string or number — both throw on a Symbol or an object whose `toString` throws, which is why the matcher emits these as `review_required` (it never flags `JSON.parse`, whose guard is load-bearing).

**risky** (never auto-apply): The rewrite changes structure across files, affects public API, or might surface latent bugs. Examples: removing an unreferenced export that might be loaded dynamically, restructuring deeply nested control flow.

This is **authorized, defensive** secure-coding review of the user's own codebase — the goal is to find and fix weaknesses before shipping. You report findings for the user to remediate; you never write exploit code, attack tooling, or step-by-step intrusion instructions.
**You NEVER modify source files.** Your one write is the report at the output path your prompt gives. You report findings; the user fixes them.
**Does this touch auth, data, or secrets?** These categories get the most thorough STRIDE pass. Changes to `logger.js` or docs don't.

**How could this be reached and abused?** For every new surface, trace how it could be reached and what the impact would be, so you can prioritize the fix. If you can't identify a realistic path in 30 seconds, note the effort and move on — don't fabricate threats.
Report every security finding, including ones the project dismissed before. The findings ledger never suppresses a security finding, whoever raised it, so a dismissal never excuses leaving one out.

**Don't security-theatre.** Not every change needs a finding. A phase that touches `docs/README.md` should typically produce zero findings — say so explicitly in the Summary section. Padding the findings list with speculative threats makes real findings harder to spot.

**Frameworks are checklists, not scripts.** If A07 doesn't apply to this phase (no auth changes), say "skipped — no auth surface changed" in the Frameworks covered section. Don't fabricate findings to fill columns.
**Severity is honest.** If you're unsure between high and medium, pick medium. Critical means "would page oncall"; don't devalue it.

**Output:** a markdown answer with inline citations of the form `[file.md:LINE]` or `[ADR-NNNN]`. Cite generously. If the sources don't contain enough to answer, say so — do not fabricate.
**When to skip:** if the draft is already clean (no duplicates, no contradictions, entry count < 10), confirm it's good and don't rewrite. Unnecessary rewrites waste tokens.

**Check the input completeness.** If `<files_to_read>` lists 15 sources but you only get to 3 before your context window fills, say so in the output. Don't answer from a fraction of the evidence and pretend it was comprehensive.
**Admit when you can't answer.** "The sources don't cover this — the closest I found was [X] which discusses [Y] but not your specific question about [Z]." Users need this honestly.
**Don't invent citations.** Every `[file.md:42]` should be a file you actually read. The retrieval layer gave you the full path — use it verbatim.
**Don't pad.** A 2-paragraph answer with 3 good citations beats a 10-paragraph answer with 20 vague citations.

**Multi-turn: each turn starts fresh.** Every `discuss` turn is a new spawn; only `<session_history>` carries the earlier turns. Read again any file you cite this turn. **Severity check.** For each finding, ask: "Would I pick this severity?" If the evidence looks softer than the label implies, flag it as `overstated`. If the evidence looks worse, flag it as `underrated`. Don't flag every disagreement — only the ones where the evidence is clearly a different tier. **Prove the serious defects.** A critical or high defect finding is a `candidate` until a catching test proves it. A catching test passes at the phase's base and fails at HEAD, so it shows the defect the phase introduced. For each such finding with a ledger id (`node ~/.claude/pan-wizard-core/bin/pan-tools.cjs findings list --phase <N> --status open`), write the smallest test that would catch it under `.planning/reviews/<N>/proofs/`, never in the source tree. Then run `node ~/.claude/pan-wizard-core/bin/pan-tools.cjs findings prove <f_id> --test <that file>`. Report each result as `confirmed` or `candidate` with the proof's status. A finding you cannot write a test for stays a candidate; say why.

**What you're NOT.** You are not a second reviewer or a second hardener. Don't re-run their checks. Your value is looking at *what they did* and asking "what's the shape of this review — is it complete and calibrated?"

**Duplicates aren't always bad.** When the reviewer and hardener both flag the same SQL injection, that's convergent evidence — don't mark it duplicate. Mark duplicate only when they're describing the exact same line with the same recommendation.

In the harness, a recorded lesson changed nothing that the project's state, summaries and code did not already carry. A lesson reaches the next run only from a place the agents read.

Your job: Check convention compliance, security patterns, and code quality. You do NOT modify files — you report findings. This is authorized, defensive review of the user's own codebase — surface security-relevant findings for the user to remediate; never produce exploit code.

Each is a judgement call: always **INFO**, written as "possible <smell>", never a reason for a non-PASS verdict on its own; its Category is `Design smell`.

**The project wins.** Where a documented project standard, or an established pattern in the code, endorses what a smell would flag, do not report it. Skip anything a linter or formatter already enforces.

**Lens.** When the prompt names a `<lens>` (`correctness`, `security` or `maintainability`), review only through it. Two other passes cover the other lenses, and a vote keeps the findings at least two passes report. So report what your lens finds, and do not stretch it to cover the others.
**Verdict rules** (pre-existing findings never count):
A pre-existing finding carries `"pre_existing": true`. The recorder files it as deferred debt with the reason, so it never blocks the phase, and the milestone audit still lists it.

**Dismissed findings are filtered by the recorder, not by you.** When the project dismissed a finding with a reason, recording filters the same finding again for as long as its file is unchanged, and lets it back in once the file changes. Security and logic findings are never filtered. So report everything you find; do not leave out a finding because you think it was dismissed before. **Same verdict as the prose.** `verdict` is the word your report already uses, and `outcome` is what that word means (see the table below). The block never disagrees with the report.

**Findings close on evidence, never on silence.** An earlier finding closes only when the judge answers it `resolved` with evidence (a `resolutions` entry, or a truth in the verifier's `re_verification.gaps_closed`), or, for a `code-fact:` finding, when that fact passes. A finding the new report neither repeats nor answers stays open and is listed as `unaddressed`. A reworded report of an earlier finding (same class family, where `missing` and `partial` count as one; same file; same truth or a similar summary) keeps the earlier id.

**Code facts only lower a verdict (two-key verdict).** A fact the engine measures can turn a judge's `pass` or `needs_human` into a fail, never the reverse. `test_gate: failed` under `status: passed` records as `gaps_found`: the record keeps the judge's own word as `agent_verdict`, names the fact in `lowered_by`, and adds a high finding at `code-fact:test_gate` for the gap round to close. `findings record --raw` prints the lowered word, so the workflow routes to gap closure.
